gloss_terse: Binnui — post-exilic proper name borne by Levites, returned exiles, and men who divorced foreign wives in Ezra-Nehemiah
gloss_readable: A Hebrew proper name meaning 'built up' (from the root בנה, 'to build'), carried by at least five individuals in the post-exilic community. One Binnui headed a family that returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 7:15), another was a Levite active in Ezra's reforms (Ezra 8:33; Neh 10:10; 12:8), and two others appear among those who had taken foreign wives (Ezra 10:30, 38). The multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name, confirming it as a single lexical identity across all occurrences.

senses.1: The proper name Binnui (בִּנּוּי), denoting several post-exilic Israelites. A family head returning under Zerubbabel (Neh 7:15, parallel to Bani in Ezra 2:10), a Levite who weighed temple vessels (Ezra 8:33) and sealed the covenant (Neh 10:10), and men who put away foreign wives (Ezra 10:30, 38). Spanish, French, and German glosses all preserve the transliteration with minimal variation (Binui, Binnui), pointing to a stable onomastic tradition.

gloss_terse: A building or constructed structure, used exclusively in Ezekiel's temple vision for walls and edifices of the eschatological sanctuary
gloss_readable: A masculine noun (בִּנְיָן) meaning 'building' or 'structure,' likely a loan-word from Aramaic. It appears only in Ezekiel's visionary temple complex (chapters 40-42), where it designates both the enclosing wall of the sacred precinct (Ezek 40:5) and the rear building behind the temple proper (Ezek 41:12, 15). The narrow distribution — all seven occurrences in a single prophetic vision — marks this as specialized architectural terminology for describing sacred space.

senses.1: A constructed edifice or architectural structure, used in Ezekiel's temple vision to describe the enclosing wall (Ezek 40:5), the rear building (Ezek 41:12, 15), and other parts of the sacred complex (Ezek 42:1, 5, 10). The multilingual evidence consistently renders it with building terms — Spanish edificio, French bâtiment, German Gebäude — confirming a concrete architectural sense rather than an abstract notion of 'construction.'

gloss_terse: Beasts, cattle, or livestock — a collective noun for domesticated animals, especially beasts of burden
gloss_readable: A collective masculine noun (בְּעִיר) denoting domesticated animals or livestock in general, with cognates across Semitic languages (Aramaic, Syriac, Ethiopic, Arabic — where it specifically denotes a camel). In Hebrew it covers beasts of burden such as donkeys (Gen 45:17, referring back to the brothers' asses) as well as cattle more broadly. It appears in legal texts governing livestock damage (Exod 22:4-5) and in wilderness narrative where Israel pleads for water for their livestock (Num 20:4, 8, 11).

senses.1: Domesticated animals or livestock viewed collectively, including beasts of burden and cattle. In Genesis 45:17, Joseph tells his brothers to load their בְּעִיר (donkeys, cf. 44:3, 13). In the Covenant Code (Exod 22:4-5), the term appears in a law about grazing damage. In Numbers 20:4, 8, 11, it covers the congregation's livestock needing water at Meribah, and in Psalm 78:48 it parallels flocks destroyed by hail. The Spanish ganado and French bétail both capture the collective 'livestock' sense.

gloss_terse: Vintage, grape harvest — the seasonal gathering of grapes from the vineyard
gloss_readable: A masculine noun (בָּצִיר) derived from the verb בָּצַר ('to cut off, gather grapes'), denoting the vintage or grape harvest. It anchors a key moment in the ancient Israelite agricultural calendar: the grape-gathering season that followed the wheat and barley harvests. In Leviticus 26:5, abundant vintage is promised as a covenant blessing — 'your threshing shall reach to the vintage.' It also serves as a metaphor for judgment and desolation, as when Micah laments being like the gleanings after vintage (Mic 7:1).

senses.1: The vintage or grape harvest, the seasonal activity of gathering ripe grapes from the vineyard. Literally denotes the harvest season in Leviticus 26:5 (the threshing reaching to the vintage as a sign of blessing) and Isaiah 32:10 (the vintage failing as judgment). Used figuratively in Isaiah 24:13 and Micah 7:1, where the gleaning after vintage symbolizes scarcity and desolation. Jeremiah 48:32 addresses Moab's vineyards whose vintage has been cut off. Spanish vendimia and French vintage both preserve the grape-harvest specificity.

gloss_terse: Pure, clean, sincere — describing moral clarity of heart, ritual cleanness, or physical emptiness
gloss_readable: An adjective (בַּר) meaning 'pure' or 'clean,' used across ethical, liturgical, and even mundane contexts. In the Psalms it describes the moral purity required to stand before God — 'clean hands and a pure heart' (Ps 24:4) and those 'pure of heart' toward whom God is good (Ps 73:1). The commands of the LORD are called בָּרָה, 'pure' (Ps 19:9). In Proverbs 14:4, it describes an empty, clean manger — no oxen means a clean crib, but also no harvest. The range from inner moral purity to physical emptiness gives this word a distinctive breadth.

senses.1: Pure, clean, or sincere, spanning moral, ritual, and physical senses. Ethically, it describes purity of heart required for worship (Ps 24:4, בַר לֵבָב 'pure in heart'; Ps 73:1, בָּרֵי לֵבָב). Applied to God's commands as flawless and pure (Ps 19:9). In Song of Songs 6:9-10, it describes a maiden as 'pure' or 'bright.' Job 11:4 uses it of personal moral claim. In Proverbs 14:4, it means physically 'clean' or 'empty' — a clean manger signals no livestock and thus no productivity. French pur and Spanish pura/limpio capture the ethical and physical dimensions respectively.

gloss_terse: Basemath — proper name ('fragrant') borne by wives of Esau and a daughter of Solomon
gloss_readable: A feminine proper name (בָּשְׂמַת) likely meaning 'fragrant' or 'perfume,' derived from the root בשׂם ('spice, balsam'). It is borne by at least two — possibly three — women in Scripture. In Genesis 26:34, Basemath is a Hittite wife of Esau (daughter of Elon), while in Genesis 36:3 a Basemath daughter of Ishmael also marries Esau, creating a well-known harmonization puzzle with the name Mahalath in Genesis 28:9. A third Basemath appears as Solomon's daughter, married to the governor Ahimaaz (1 Kings 4:15).

senses.1: The proper name Basemath (בָּשְׂמַת, 'fragrant'), referring to: (1) a Hittite woman, daughter of Elon, wife of Esau (Gen 26:34); (2) a daughter of Ishmael and wife of Esau (Gen 36:3, 4, 10, 13, 17 — the Samaritan Pentateuch reads Mahalath throughout Genesis 36, reflecting a textual tradition that harmonized the names); and (3) a daughter of Solomon who married Ahimaaz (1 Kgs 4:15). Spanish Basemat/Basmat and German Basemat/Basmat preserve the Semitic root with slight orthographic variation.

gloss_terse: To rise up, grow high, be exalted — of waters rising, plants growing, or God triumphing gloriously
gloss_readable: A Qal verb (גָּאָה) meaning 'to rise up' or 'be exalted,' covering natural phenomena and divine triumph. Its most celebrated use is the Song of the Sea — 'I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously' (Exod 15:1, 21), where the cognate accusative construction גָּאֹה גָּאָה intensifies the verb into a shout of cosmic victory. Elsewhere the same verb describes rising waters in Ezekiel's temple river (Ezek 47:5) and rushes growing without water (Job 8:11), grounding divine exaltation in the observable world of things that surge upward.

senses.1: To rise up, grow, or be exalted, used across literal and figurative contexts. Of waters rising: Ezekiel's temple river that had risen (גָּאוּ) to swimming depth (Ezek 47:5). Of plants growing: Job 8:11 asks whether rushes can grow (יִגְאֶה) without water. Of divine triumph: the iconic Song of the Sea (Exod 15:1, 21) with its intensifying cognate accusative גָּאֹה גָּאָה, 'he has triumphed gloriously.' Of Job's head being lifted up under divine scrutiny (Job 10:16). Spanish ensalzar ('to exalt') and French s'élever ('to rise') together capture the dual physical and theological dimensions.

gloss_terse: To blaspheme, revile — speaking with contempt against God or reproaching others (Piel only)
gloss_readable: A verb used exclusively in the Piel stem (גִּדֵּף), meaning to revile or blaspheme — to speak with cutting contempt, whether against God or against people. The Arabic cognate جَدَفَ ('to cut, cut off') reveals the metaphorical origin: blasphemy as verbal violence that severs the bond of reverence. In Numbers 15:30, the one who acts 'with a high hand' blasphemes the LORD and is cut off from Israel. In 2 Kings 19:22 (= Isa 37:23), Hezekiah quotes God rebuking Sennacherib: 'Whom have you reviled and blasphemed?'

senses.1: To revile or blaspheme, speaking contemptuously against God or reproaching fellow humans. In Numbers 15:30, the deliberate sinner 'blasphemes the LORD' (מְגַדֵּף, participial) and must be cut off. Sennacherib's arrogance is condemned with this verb in 2 Kings 19:6, 22 and its parallel Isaiah 37:6, 23, paired with חֵרֵף ('to reproach'). Between humans, Psalm 44:17 describes the voice of one who 'reproaches and reviles' (מְחָרֵף וּמְגַדֵּף). Ezekiel 20:27 adds a further accusation of blasphemy against God. Spanish blasfemar directly mirrors the theological weight of this term.

gloss_terse: Gedor — a town in Judah's hill country and a proper name in Benjamite and Judahite genealogies
gloss_readable: A proper name (גְּדוֹר / גְּדֹר) related to the Arabic جِدَارٌ ('wall'), suggesting a walled settlement. It designates both a place and persons. As a town, Gedor appears among the cities of Judah's hill country (Josh 15:58). In the Chronicler's genealogies, Gedor is listed as a 'son' of Penuel (1 Chr 4:4) and of Jered (1 Chr 4:18) — likely eponymous founders of the town. A Benjamite named Gedor of Gibeon also appears (1 Chr 8:31; 9:37). In 1 Chronicles 4:39 the text reads Gedor, though many scholars emend to Gerar.

senses.1: The proper name Gedor, functioning as both a toponym and a personal name. As a place: a town in Judah's hill country (Josh 15:58), possibly also the location mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:39 (though LXX and many scholars read 'Gerar'). As personal names in Chronicler genealogies: a descendant of Judah through Penuel (1 Chr 4:4) and Jered (1 Chr 4:18), likely eponymous ancestors of the town. A Benjamite named Gedor appears at Gibeon (1 Chr 8:31; 9:37). The Arabic cognate جدار ('wall') suits a fortified settlement in the Judean highlands.

gloss_terse: A cub or whelp, especially of a lion — used metaphorically for tribal vigor, young warriors, and fierce offspring
gloss_readable: A masculine noun (גּוּר) meaning 'cub' or 'whelp,' primarily designating a young lion. Jacob blesses Judah as a 'lion's cub' (גּוּר אַרְיֵה, Gen 49:9), and Dan is called a 'lion's cub that leaps from Bashan' (Deut 33:22) — both evoking youthful ferocity and tribal promise. Ezekiel's allegory of the lioness (Ezek 19:2, 3, 5) uses the term for the princes of Israel raised among her cubs. In Lamentations 4:3, it extends beyond lions to describe the young of jackals (תַּנִּין), showing the word can denote any predator's offspring.

senses.1: A cub or whelp, typically of a lion, used in poetic and prophetic metaphor. Jacob's blessing calls Judah a 'lion's cub' (Gen 49:9, גּוּר אַרְיֵה), evoking tribal strength and royal destiny. Moses blesses Dan as a 'lion's cub leaping from Bashan' (Deut 33:22). In Ezekiel 19:2-5, a lioness raises her cubs (גּוּרֶיהָ) — an allegory for Judah's royal house — and one cub becomes a young lion (כְּפִיר). Nahum 2:12 pictures Nineveh's ruin through lion imagery. Lamentations 4:3 uniquely applies the term to jackal young, broadening its zoological range. Spanish cachorro ('cub') matches the core sense precisely.
